source: Koopman (1946) Search and Screening, OEG Report 56 (via Wikipedia, Bernard Koopman)
finding: Koopman, in the WWII US Navy anti-submarine group (ASWORG, led by Morse), built the first theory of searching for a hidden target. The work was confidential until declassified in 1958.
numbers: Born 1900, died 1981. First edition 1946 (confidential). Declassified 1958. Three open articles planned after 1955.
limits: Wikipedia page does not describe lateral range curves or the random search formula. Detail of the models is not confirmed here.
agent_relevance: Search theory began as a cost-limited allocation of effort under uncertainty. This is the root of 'where to look when looking costs'.

source: Bayesian search theory (Wikipedia)
finding: A search keeps a probability map over places. After an empty look in one cell the map is updated with Bayes' rule. Other cells go up, the searched cell goes down.
numbers: With prior p in a cell and detection chance q: new p' = p(1-q)/(1-pq). Every other cell with prior r becomes r/(1-pq).
limits: Needs a correct detection model. If q is overestimated, the true cell is wrongly dropped.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an agent that checks one hypothesis or source and must re-weight the rest after a failed check.

source: Bayesian search theory (Wikipedia): searching in boxes
finding: Optimal rule for a hidden object in boxes: always look in the box with the highest ratio p_i*a_i/c_i (prior probability times detection chance over cost). Blackwell solved one object, Assaf extended to many.
numbers: Rule is the index p_i*a_i/c_i. It is a special case of the Gittins index.
limits: One hidden object, independent boxes, no reward for partial finds. Extraction of the formula from the page was garbled; read as p_i a_i / c_i.
agent_relevance: Gives a ranking rule for which check to run next: cheap and likely-to-reveal first, not just most-likely.

source: Stone (1975) Theory of Optimal Search; Stone (1989); Stone et al (2011) Air France 447 (via Wikipedia)
finding: Stone's book won the 1975 Lanchester Prize and made Bayesian search a standard tool. The method was used to find USS Scorpion and helped recover Air France 447 flight recorders.
numbers: Scorpion lost May 1968, found end Oct 1968, about 740 km (400 nmi) SW of the Azores, under over 3,000 m of water. AF447 crashed 2009.
limits: Wikipedia gives few details of the actual search maths and no success rate.
agent_relevance: Evidence that probability-map search works in practice, not only in theory.

source: Stigler (1961) The Economics of Information (via Wikipedia Search theory)
finding: Stigler framed search for prices and jobs as an economic problem. In his fixed-sample model the buyer picks n quotes ahead of time to minimise expected price plus n times the cost per quote.
numbers: Price distribution F(p) on [0,1]; one-variable optimisation for sample size n.
limits: Simultaneous (non-adaptive) sample is not optimal when a searcher can look one at a time. Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Separates 'decide budget up front' from 'decide after each look'. Our agent should do the second.

source: Stigler (1962) Information in the labor market, JPE 70(5)
finding: Stigler measured pay dispersion for equal workers and said search continues until expected marginal return equals marginal cost of search.
numbers: 44 Chicago MBA graduates got 144 corporate offers (1960-61). SD of monthly offers $43, mean $540.7, coefficient of variation 7.9%. Average 2.25 offers per student. National Endicott survey: CV 6.4-9.1% for non-engineers, about 4.0-4.3% for engineers. Dispersion is about 5-10% even in a well organised market.
quote: A worker will search for wage offers until the expected marginal return equals the marginal cost of search.
limits: Dispersion measured on starting salaries only. Non-wage job traits unobserved. Small single-school sample. Text came from scanned-PDF OCR.
agent_relevance: Stop rule in one line: stop when the next look's expected gain is below its cost. Same shape as the S0 gate.

source: McCall (1970) Economics of information and job search, QJE 84(1) (via Wikipedia Search theory)
finding: McCall modelled an unemployed worker as an optimal stopping problem with a known offer distribution. The best policy is a reservation wage: reject below, accept above.
numbers: Higher variance of offers raises the reservation wage and prolongs search even for a risk-averse searcher, since bad offers can be refused.
limits: Assumes known fixed offer distribution and constant value of money. Reservation wage falls with time if the worker loses skills or runs out of money. Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: A constant threshold is the optimal stop rule in a stationary world. Threshold should fall as budget shrinks.

source: McCall (1965) Economics of information and optimal stopping rules, J Business 38(3) (via Wikipedia Search theory)
finding: First paper to bring sequential optimal stopping into the economics of search. Sequential search lets the buyer choose to stop after each quote.
limits: Wikipedia says sequential models assume the buyer already knows the quality standard and cannot learn about the distribution while searching.
agent_relevance: Learning the distribution during search is the missing piece for real agents.

source: Search-and-matching extension (Wikipedia Search theory)
finding: Macro economists extended search to general equilibrium (matching theory). Small supply imbalances can give all the gains to one side.
numbers: In a marriage market with slightly more men than women, all matching rents go to women.
limits: Wikipedia page flagged as needing more citations.
agent_relevance: Background only. Shows search effects are sensitive to small imbalances.

source: Weitzman (1979) Optimal search for the best alternative, Econometrica, as stated in Kleinberg, Waggoner and Weyl (2016)
finding: Pandora's box. Each box i has an opening cost c_i and a random prize. Give each box a reservation value sigma_i solving E[(v_i - sigma_i)+] = c_i. Open boxes in decreasing sigma and stop when the best prize found beats every unopened sigma.
numbers: Defining equation E_i(v_i - sigma_i)+ = c_i. Theorem 1: this procedure achieves first-best welfare E[max_i min(sigma_i, v_i)].
quote: stopping when the largest observed value exceeds all remaining sigma
limits: Boxes independent. Opening cost paid even if the prize is taken. Inspection is instant. Read through a secondary statement, not Weitzman's own paper.
agent_relevance: The cleanest known rule for many costly checks of unknown value. Index per check, sort, stop when best-so-far beats all remaining indices.

source: Kleinberg, Waggoner, Weyl (2016) Descending price optimally coordinates search
finding: Reads Weitzman's index as a real option: the strike price is the highest price at which paying to look is still worth it. A descending-price procedure makes many bidders reproduce the optimal search.
numbers: Strike price sigma: E[(v-sigma)+]=c. Covered-call value min(sigma, v). Welfare equals E[max covered-call value].
limits: Risk-neutral, independent values, quasilinear utility.
agent_relevance: The option-value view: look at a thing only if its upside beyond the current best is worth its price.

source: Chawla, Gergatsouli, Teng, Tzamos, Zhang (2020) Pandora's Box with Correlations
finding: First approximation algorithms for Pandora's box when box values are correlated and only samples of the joint distribution are known. Fully adaptive strategies cannot be approximated within any sub-linear factor from samples.
numbers: Main result: constant-factor approximation to the best partially adaptive (fixed order, adaptive stop) strategy with polynomial samples. Constants proved tight.
limits: Weitzman's independence assumption fails in real settings. Results are for sample access to the joint law. Only abstract and intro read closely.
agent_relevance: Our agent's checks are correlated. A fixed good order plus an adaptive stop is the safe design.

source: Gittins index (Wikipedia)
finding: Gittins and Jones (1979): the best policy for the discounted bandit is to play the arm with the highest index, defined as sup over stopping times of expected discounted reward divided by expected discounted time. Weitzman reached the same idea independently in search.
numbers: Whittle: index is a Lagrange multiplier. Restless-bandit version is NP-complete in general. Katehakis-Veinott restart-in-state gives exact computation.
limits: No numbers for discount factors on the page.
agent_relevance: Search with learning (bandit) and search with a fixed distribution (Pandora) share an index form.

source: Secretary problem (Wikipedia)
finding: With n candidates in random order and no recall, reject the first n/e and take the next best-so-far. This picks the single best with probability about 1/e.
numbers: Win probability about 0.368 as n grows. Exact: n=2 0.500, n=3 0.500, n=4 0.458, n=5 0.433, n=10 0.399; optimal cutoff r = 1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4 for n=1..10. Second best goal: 1/4. Cardinal payoff uniform on [0,1]: expected value of t-th candidate given it is a candidate t/(t+1).
limits: Rank-only information. With cardinal values the cutoff is earlier. Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Baseline for 'when to stop browsing options': sample a fraction, then commit.

source: Seale and Rapoport; Bearden (via Wikipedia Secretary problem)
finding: People tend to stop earlier than the 1/e rule, partly because evaluating candidates has a cost.
numbers: Wikipedia gives no numbers for these experiments.
limits: Only the qualitative claim from the review page was read. Original experiments not opened, so effect sizes are unknown.
agent_relevance: Humans under-search relative to the optimum. Whether LLMs do the same is untested here.

source: Optimal stopping (Wikipedia)
finding: Optimal stopping problems are solved with the Bellman equation and dynamic programming. House-selling example: a sale on day n yields X_n - n*k with k the daily advertising cost. Search theory is the worker or consumer case.
numbers: Compact form for the jump-diffusion case: max{ A phi + L, M - phi } = 0.
limits: Page gives no experiment and no Moser result.
agent_relevance: Search is an optimal stopping problem. The Bellman form is what an S0 gate should approximate.

source: Charnov (1976) marginal value theorem; reviewed on Wikipedia
finding: A forager should leave a patch when its current capture rate falls to the average rate over the whole environment, travel included. Geometric form: tangent line from the travel-time point.
numbers: Great tits (Naef-Daenzer 1999): foraging about 30% better than random. Yellow dung flies (Parker 1999): predicted copulation 40 min, observed 36 min. Cowie 1977 great tits: qualitative support only. Cassini 1990 armadillos and guinea pigs: patches exploited further than predicted.
limits: Animals often stay longer than the theory says. No human cognitive search numbers on the page.
agent_relevance: Stop rule for depth on one idea: leave when marginal gain falls below the average gain per unit time.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 in multi-armed bandits mostly fail to explore. Only GPT-4 with a hint to explore, externally summarised per-arm averages and chain of thought explores well.
numbers: GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure (best arm never chosen after some step) in more than 60% of replicates. 48 configurations each for GPT-3.5 and Llama2, 72 for GPT-4. T=100 mostly, 20 replicates for GPT-3.5, about 10 for most GPT-4. Only one configuration worked. Baselines UCB, Thompson sampling, Greedy with 1000 replicates.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small bandit instances, 2023-24 models, T=100 mostly. External summarising may not scale.
agent_relevance: Search with learning is hard for LLMs. The scaffold should keep sufficient statistics outside the model and force a look at under-sampled options.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 beats humans on a multi-armed bandit task but shows no directed exploration in Wilson's horizon task.
numbers: Horizon task: GPT-3 short-horizon regret indistinguishable from humans (t(5566) = -0.043, p=.97). Long-horizon initial regret lower than humans (t(5550) = -4.07, p<.001). Decisions from descriptions on 13,000 problems: largest model did not reach human level (t(29134) = -11.50, p<.001).
limits: GPT-3 (2022). Human data taken from other studies, not run in parallel.
agent_relevance: Information value is not used: the model does not look more when more looks remain.

source: Li et al (2024) Escape sky-high cost: Early-stopping self-consistency, ICLR 2024
finding: A stop rule for sampling: draw answers in windows and stop when all answers in one window agree. It saves many samples at almost the same accuracy.
numbers: Max samples L=64 for MATH, 40 elsewhere; window 8 for MATH, 5 otherwise. Average samples cut by 33.8% (MATH), 80.1% (GSM8K), 76.8% (StrategyQA), 78.5% (CSQA), 84.2% (Coin Flip), 67.4% (Last Letters). GPT-4 MATH: SC 60.32%, ESC 60.32%. Sample-matched SC lost up to about 30 points on weaker models.
limits: Stop rule is an agreement heuristic, not derived from a cost model. 10 runs averaged, variance omitted.
agent_relevance: A working LLM stop rule for repeated sampling. Stopping early on easy items pays.

source: Brown et al (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction solved by any of k samples) rises smoothly with k over four orders of magnitude, near log-linear, fit by an exponentiated power law. Picking the right answer without a verifier plateaus.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (single-sample state of the art 43%). CodeContests, Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples. MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Needs an automatic verifier to turn coverage into accuracy. 128 problems each for GSM8K and MATH.
agent_relevance: Search pays when finding is cheap and recognising is easy. The verifier is the bottleneck, so build checks before widening the search.

source: Yao et al (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Treat reasoning as search over partial solutions with breadth-first or depth-first search and a model-based value check. Large gain on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: chain of thought 4% solved, ToT 74%.
quote: in Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%
limits: Costs many more calls per problem. No per-call cost accounting in what was read.
agent_relevance: Structured search with a pruning check beats a single path where lookahead matters.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally
finding: How best to spend inference compute depends on prompt difficulty. Allocating adaptively per prompt beats a fixed best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy gives more than 4x better efficiency than best-of-N. In FLOPs-matched tests a smaller model with extra test-time compute beats a 14x larger one on questions where the small model has non-trivial success.
limits: Only abstract and intro read closely. On the hardest questions extra test-time compute helped less than more pretraining. PaLM 2-S* on MATH.
agent_relevance: This is search budgeting for LLMs: estimate difficulty, then decide how much to search. It supports an S0 gate.

source: Stigler (1962) year-to-year persistence of offers
finding: Stigler checks whether pay differences between firms persist. If they persist, searching keeps paying.
numbers: Correlation of company salary offers across years for engineers: 0.660 (1958 vs 1959), 0.761 (1959 vs 1960), 0.577 (1958 vs 1960).
limits: Three years of one survey. Diamond's 1971 paradox page could not be opened (404).
agent_relevance: Dispersion is what makes searching pay. If all options look equal the search gate should close.

source: Doval (2014); Olszewski and Weber (2015); Weber (1992), as cited in KWW (2016)
finding: KWW cite Doval 'Whether or not to open Pandora's box' and Olszewski and Weber 'A more general Pandora's rule?' as extensions of Weitzman, and Weber (1992) for the Gittins prevailing-charge proof.
numbers: Reference list only.
limits: Only references seen, not the papers.
agent_relevance: Pointers for Angle B: non-obligatory inspection variants.
